reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and Design Methods (2018)

sections.title: Axial Load Transfer
sections.body: Drilled shafts transmit axial compression and uplift loads through side resistance Rs and base (tip) resistance RB. Load transfer mechanics (Kulhawy 1991, O'Neill and Reese 1972): Side resistance mobilized first at small displacements (~1/2 inch for full mobilization); base resistance mobilizes at larger displacements (~4-5% of diameter B for cohesive soil and rock; ~10% B for cohesionless soils). Three components: side resistance Rs, base resistance RB, and combined total resistance QT. Between peak side and peak base resistance, side resistance may increase or decrease depending on stress-strain behavior at shaft-soil interface (softening possible in some materials). Design for service limit states must account for differences in mobilization displacement for side vs. base resistance.
key_points: Side resistance mobilizes at ~1/2 inch displacement; base resistance at ~4-10% of shaft diameter
Displacement for maximum base resistance: 4-5% B (cohesive/rock) or 10% B (cohesionless)
Side resistance mobilizes first; peak side and peak base occur at different displacements
Service limit state design must account for differences in side vs. base mobilization

sections.title: Relationship to Overall Design Process
sections.body: Chapter constitutes detailed treatment of Block 11 ('Establish Minimum Depth and Diameter for Axial Loads') of the overall design process (Figure 8-1, Chapter 8). AASHTO (2017a) identifies axial compression and uplift of single drilled shafts as strength limit states; settlement control as service limit state. Factored axial force effects communicated by structural engineer to foundation designer for each applicable limit state and scour condition. For cohesive soils in Service I load combination, transient loads can be omitted from settlement analysis.
key_points: Block 11 of overall design process: minimum depth and diameter for axial loads
Strength limit states: axial compression and uplift
Service limit state: settlement control
Transient loads may be omitted from settlement analysis in cohesive soils
sections.applicability: Relates axial design to overall design process; limit state identification

sections.title: Step-by-Step Procedure: Design for Axial Load
sections.body: [pp. 10-3 to 10-4] A step-by-step LRFD procedure for drilled shafts under axial loading, depicted in the simplified flow chart of Figure 10-2 and an expanded description of Block 11 of the overall design process (Figure 8-1): (1) at each foundation location divide the subsurface strata into a finite number of geomaterial layers and assign each one type: cohesionless soil, cohesive soil or rock; (2) review the strength and service limit states to be satisfied and establish the corresponding axial load combinations and load factors for each foundation; (3) for each layer and each limit state/load case assign the geomaterial properties needed for the axial resistances; (4) select trial lengths and diameters, the minimum trial diameter possibly governed by lateral load (Chapter 9) or structural requirements (Chapter 12); (5) compute nominal unit side resistance for all layers the trial shaft passes through and nominal unit base resistance at the trial tip elevation; (6) iterating from Step 4 as necessary, adjust the trial design to satisfy the LRFD requirement for each strength limit state, Sum(eta_i gamma_i F_i) <= Sum(phi_i R_i) (Eq. 10-1), its parameters defined in Chapter 8 and resistance factors selected per AASHTO guidelines and agency experience; (7) conduct load-deformation analysis for each trial design and iterate from Step 4 as necessary to satisfy each service limit state, analyzing the side and base resistances mobilized at the axial displacement equal to the tolerable deformation of the structure. The results are combined with design for other loading modes (lateral, extreme events, structural) in the overall procedure of Chapter 8; details and examples of each step follow (10.3.1 to 10.3.8).
key_points: Seven steps: layers and types; limit states and loads; properties; trial dimensions; unit resistances; strength check; service check
Geomaterial types: cohesionless soil, cohesive soil, rock
Minimum trial diameter may be set by lateral load (Chapter 9) or structural needs (Chapter 12)
Strength check: Sum(eta gamma F) <= Sum(phi R) (Eq. 10-1); iterate from Step 4
Service check: resistances mobilized at the tolerable deformation

sections.title: Idealized Geomaterial Layer Profiles (Step 1)
sections.body: [pp. 10-4 to 10-6] A design zone is an area where one or more drilled shafts will be installed and for which an idealized geomaterial layer profile is developed, e.g., a single bridge pier on one or more shafts, or each shaft if a boring is made at every shaft location. In each profile (Figure 10-3) each layer is assigned a number i, thickness Delta z_i and geomaterial type: (a) cohesionless soil, USCS GW, GP, GM, SW, SP, SM and ML (gravels and sands with less than 5 percent fines, gravels and sands with silty fines, and non-plastic silts); (b) cohesive soil, GC, SC, CL, CH and MH (clayey sands and gravels, lean and fat clays, and silts with liquid limit over 50); (c) rock, cohesive cemented geomaterial identified as rock on the basis of geologic origin. Dual classifications such as SM-SC and ML-CL may need laboratory direct shear or triaxial tests to decide whether drained or undrained loading governs; special or regionally important geomaterials are treated in Appendix B, and load testing with locally calibrated resistance factors is recommended for unusual or 'non-textbook' geomaterials. Scour is taken into account in the profiles: all resistances for strength and service limit states are evaluated for the scour design flood, while scour from the more severe scour design check flood is an extreme event. Scour changes subsurface stress, reduces embedment and so axial and lateral resistances, and may change the superstructure response and foundation force effects (Section 10.5; effects on axial resistance in 10.5.5). A spreadsheet or other tool is recommended at this stage, listing each layer's number, thickness and type, to which properties and side and base resistances are added in later steps.
key_points: Design zone: one pier, or each shaft where each has a boring
Cohesionless: GW, GP, GM, SW, SP, SM, ML; cohesive: GC, SC, CL, CH, MH; rock by geologic origin
Dual classes (SM-SC, ML-CL) may need lab strength tests to choose drained or undrained analysis
Unusual geomaterials: Appendix B; load tests and local resistance factors
Strength and service resistances use the scour design flood; the check flood is an extreme event

sections.title: Limit States and Factored Axial Loads (Step 2)
sections.body: [p. 10-6] For axial loading, Step 2 reviews the limit states, load combinations, load factors and scour conditions that pertain specifically to axial loading, as discussed in Section 10.2 and Chapter 8, and requires direct communication between the structural engineer and the foundation designer.
key_points: Review axial limit states, load combinations, load factors and scour conditions (10.2, Chapter 8)
Requires direct communication between structural engineer and foundation designer
sections.applicability: Establishing the axial limit states and factored loads for drilled shaft design

sections.title: Geomaterial Properties (Step 3)
sections.body: [pp. 10-6 to 10-7] For each layer the designer assigns the properties needed to evaluate side and base resistances (Table 10-1) for the methods of Section 10.3.5. Cohesionless soils are evaluated as fully drained, with no distinction between short- and long-term conditions. Cohesive soils are evaluated as undrained for short-term (end of construction) loading and fully drained for long-term loading; under most conditions the short-term undrained resistance is critical (less than the drained), so resistances are evaluated from su. Drained conditions may be worth considering, e.g., where a substantial portion of the shaft penetrates very heavily overconsolidated clay (OCR > 8) in which negative pore pressures can develop under short-term loading; then both are analyzed and the smaller resistance governs. In a layered profile the short-term resistance uses effective stress for cohesionless layers and total stress for cohesive layers; if the long-term drained response is critical, all layers are evaluated in effective stress. LRFD uses mean property values for each layer: compute the mean, standard deviation and COV (e.g., in a spreadsheet), plot each property with depth with a linear trend line, and select the value at layer mid-depth. To apply the Table 8-4 resistance factors the COV should not exceed 45 percent for N-values within a layer and 35 percent for undrained shear strength of a cohesive layer (CU or UU triaxial tests); otherwise obtain more data or reduce the resistance factors by judgment, and consider splitting the layer into sub-layers.
key_points: Cohesionless: drained always; cohesive: undrained short-term usually critical, evaluated from su
Consider drained analysis too in very heavily overconsolidated clay (OCR > 8); smaller resistance governs
Use mean values at layer mid-depth from a trend line with depth
COV limits for Table 8-4 factors: 45 percent for N-values, 35 percent for su; else more data, lower phi or split layers

(1) Long-term fully drained axial resistance in cohesive soils is not considered in AASHTO (2017) LRFD Specifications, design for undrained loading being assumed adequate for routine practice

sections.title: Select Trial Lengths and Diameters (Step 4)
sections.body: [pp. 10-7 to 10-8] Trial depths and diameters are selected for the axial force effects of each limit state from Step 2, starting from any lateral design (Chapter 9), with experience and knowledge of the ground. Rules of thumb: L/B generally 3 to 30; in soil, depths to 100 ft and diameters up to 8 ft are routine for construction in most cases; depths to 200 ft and diameters up to 12 ft are within the range of well-equipped specialty subcontractors but with increased construction risk; rock sockets up to 50 ft are possible but seldom warranted, common socket diameter B ≤ 5 ft; sockets of 8 ft and larger are within the range of well-equipped, experienced specialty subcontractors; deeper and larger shafts are possible at premium cost and with major construction challenges; limiting depth to allow the dry method generally favors cost and inspection; a larger diameter may help remove boulders or rock fragments; structural considerations may govern, the shaft typically slightly larger than the column for installation tolerance, larger to reduce reinforcement congestion, with continuous or spliced reinforcement, in close consultation with the structural engineer; minimum concrete cover ranges from 3 to 6 inches depending on diameter (Chapter 6, project specifications, Chapter 14); overburden diameter at least 6 inches larger than the rock socket for rock drilling equipment; and for sign structures, a diameter large enough for the bearing or anchor plate. Where rock is within practical excavation depth, the base may sit on the rock, in a socket, or the shaft may 'float' above it; where all limit states can be met and scour is not an issue the most economical design usually avoids rock excavation, unless adequate resistance cannot be developed even with a very large diameter (say, up to 12 ft) and rock is close to the surface. Bearing on versus socketing depends on rock quality near the overburden interface, severe slope of the rock, and whether adequate resistance is possible without a socket; highly weathered, karstic or severely sloping rock, or scour down close to the rock surface, usually calls for a socket. In massive hard rock (e.g., qu ≥ 10,000 psi) socketing is slow and costly, and a larger shaft bearing on the rock surface, or 6 to 12 inches into it to seal a casing, may be reasonable. A single large shaft is generally more cost effective than a group, with exceptions such as difficult access on steep slopes (smaller equipment instead of temporary walls or a trestle) or multiple small rock sockets; sometimes both options must be designed and compared on cost and constructability (groups in Chapter 11).
key_points: L/B generally 3 to 30
Soil: to 100 ft deep and 8 ft diameter routine; to 200 ft and 12 ft for specialty subcontractors
Rock sockets up to 50 ft possible, seldom warranted; common socket B ≤ 5 ft; 8 ft and larger for specialists
Cover 3 to 6 inches by diameter; overburden shaft at least 6 inches larger than the socket
Avoid rock excavation where all limit states are met and scour is not an issue
Massive hard rock (qu ≥ 10,000 psi): bear on the surface or 6 to 12 inches in rather than a small socket
Single shaft usually cheaper than a group; compare where access or rock favors several small shafts
sections.applicability: Choosing trial shaft dimensions and whether to bear on, socket into or float above rock

sections.title: Calculate Nominal Side and Base Resistances (Step 5)
sections.body: [p. 10-9] This step calculates the geotechnical resistances for axial compression or uplift loads. The methods are those of Article 10.8 of the 2017 AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications, unless research supported by full-scale axial load tests warrants a different approach. For the two components of compression resistance (side and base), the summation of factored resistances on the right side of Equation 10-1 is: Sum(phi_i R_i) = Sum over i = 1 to n of phi_S,i R_SN,i + phi_B R_BN (Eq. 10-2), where R_SN,i is the nominal side resistance of layer i, phi_S,i the resistance factor for side resistance in layer i, n the number of layers providing side resistance, R_BN the nominal base resistance and phi_B the resistance factor for base resistance. Nominal side resistance of a layer is the nominal unit side resistance f_SN times the cylindrical area, layer thickness Delta z_i times the circumference: R_SN = pi B Delta z_i f_SN (Eq. 10-3), with B the shaft diameter. Nominal base resistance is the nominal unit base resistance q_BN times the area at the base: R_BN = (pi B^2 / 4) q_BN (Eq. 10-4). Nominal unit side resistance is evaluated in effective stress for cohesionless soil layers; in total stress for end-of-construction (undrained) conditions in cohesive soil layers (effective stress analysis if the long-term, fully drained side resistance is important); and in terms of uniaxial compressive strength in rock. The methods for each category of geomaterial follow in 10.3.5.1 (cohesionless soils), 10.3.5.2 (cohesive soils) and 10.3.5.3 (rock).
key_points: Eq. 10-2: sum of factored resistances = sum of phi_S,i R_SN,i over the n side layers + phi_B R_BN
Eq. 10-3: R_SN = pi B (Delta z_i) f_SN; Eq. 10-4: R_BN = (pi B^2/4) q_BN
Side resistance: effective stress in cohesionless soil, total stress (undrained, end of construction) in cohesive soil, uniaxial compressive strength in rock
Methods follow Article 10.8 of the 2017 AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications
equations: Eq. 10-2: Sum(phi_i R_i) = Sum[i=1..n](phi_S,i R_SN,i) + phi_B R_BN — factored axial compression resistance
Eq. 10-3: R_SN = pi B (Delta z_i) f_SN — nominal side resistance of layer i
Eq. 10-4: R_BN = (pi B^2 / 4) q_BN — nominal base resistance
sections.applicability: Nominal side and base resistance of drilled shafts in compression or uplift; the geomaterial-specific methods are in 10.3.5.1 to 10.3.5.3

sections.title: Cohesionless Soils
sections.body: SIDE RESISTANCE [p. 10-10]. Nominal side resistance is the frictional resistance over the cylindrical soil-shaft interface; the unit side resistance is proportional to the normal stress on the interface (Figure 10-4). By Equation 10-3: R_SN = pi B Delta z f_SN = pi B Delta z (sigma'_v K tan delta) (Eq. 10-5), where sigma'_v is the average vertical effective stress over Delta z, K = sigma'_h/sigma'_v is the coefficient of horizontal soil stress, sigma'_h the horizontal effective stress, and delta the effective stress angle of friction for the soil-shaft interface. Combining terms: beta = K tan delta (Eq. 10-6) and f_SN = sigma'_v beta (Eq. 10-7); beta is the side resistance coefficient (the 'beta method'). Chen and Kulhawy (2002) evaluate K and delta separately and then combine them to beta. [p. 10-11] K is a function of the at-rest value K_o and of the change in horizontal stress caused by construction, K/K_o. A first-order approximation is K/K_o = 1 (no stress change from construction). For 'normal' (uncemented) soils K_o follows Mayne and Kulhawy (1982): K_o = (1 - sin phi') OCR^(sin phi') <= K_p (Eq. 10-8), with OCR = sigma'_p / sigma'_v (Eq. 10-9), sigma'_p the effective vertical preconsolidation stress, and K_p = tan^2(45 deg + phi'/2) (Eq. 10-10) the upper bound. From SPT N-values, Mayne (2007): sigma'_p / p_a ~ 0.47 (N60)^m (Eq. 10-11), with m = 0.6 for clean quartzitic sands and m = 0.8 for silty sands to sandy silts (e.g., Piedmont residual soils), p_a atmospheric pressure in the units of sigma'_p (e.g., 2,116 psf). For gravelly soils, Kulhawy and Chen (2007): sigma'_p / p_a = 0.15 N60 (Eq. 10-12). Substituting Eqs. 10-9 to 10-12 into Eq. 10-6 gives beta ~ (1 - sin phi') (sigma'_p / sigma'_v)^(sin phi') tan phi' <= K_p tan phi' (Eq. 10-13), with sigma'_p from Eq. 10-11 for sandy soils and Eq. 10-12 for gravelly soils. [pp. 10-11, 10-12] beta at shallow depth is limited to its value at a depth of 7.5 ft, a vertical effective stress of about 900 psf; at lower confining stress the correlations for friction angle and preconsolidation stress are not validated. beta from Eq. 10-13 goes into Eq. 10-7 for the unit side resistance and into Eq. 10-5 for R_SN of each cohesionless layer. The principal limitation is the reliance on N-values and their correlations with friction angle and preconsolidation stress. Resistance factors have not been established for this method by a probability-based calibration with the AASHTO LRFD load factors; calibration to ASD with a factor of safety FS = 2.5 gives phi_S = 0.55 for side resistance in cohesionless soils, recommended until a reliability-based calibration is done. The method assumes no change in K from construction, which holds for dry, slurry (wet-hole) and casing methods with minimal sidewall disturbance, proper handling of slurry and casing and prompt concrete placement; otherwise K can fall to 2/3 of K_o, or lower if the soil caves. Where permanent casing extends through cohesionless soil, AASHTO (2007a) states no specific data are available but casing reduction factors of 0.60 to 0.75 are commonly used; side resistance may be neglected over the depth of permanent casing in very soft soils or where scour is expected. Scour: all material above the total scour line is assumed removed, and the change in stress affects beta (Section 10.5). ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE 10-1 [pp. 10-12 to 10-14]: shaft B = 5 ft; layer 1 (0 to 15 ft, N60 = 9, (N1)60 = 14, gamma = 115 pcf) and layer 2 (15 to 33 ft, N60 = 27, (N1)60 = 28, gamma_sat = 125 pcf) of silty sand. The friction angle is taken as phi' = delta = 27.5 + 9.2 log[(N1)60] = 38 deg and 41 deg (Chen and Kulhawy, 2002), so delta = phi'. sigma'_v at mid-layer 862.5 and 2,288.4 psf; sigma'_p = 2,116 x 0.47 (N60)^0.8 = 5,768 and 13,890 psf; OCR 6.7 and 6.1; K_o 1.24 and 1.13 (K_p 4.20 and 4.81); beta = K tan delta = 0.97 and 0.98; f_SN = 837 and 2,248 psf (the printed layer 2 line shows beta as 1.08 while the printed summary table gives 0.98); R_SN,1 = 197.2 kips, R_SN,2 = 635.6 kips, sum 833 kips. BASE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-14, 10-15]. Base resistance develops with downward displacement, and the displacement for full mobilization varies widely because excavation releases stress beneath the base and base cleaning varies; direct empirical correlation with SPT N-values from load tests is recommended for routine design (Reese and O'Neill, 1989): q_BN (tsf) = 0.60 N60 <= 30 tsf (Eq. 10-14), N60 the average between the base and two diameters below it, the field value with no overburden correction (at 60 percent hammer efficiency). It rests on compression tests on shafts with clean bases at settlements of five percent of the base diameter; the 30 tsf limit is the largest value in those tests. It applies to cohesionless soils with N-values of 50 blows per foot or less; above 50, load testing is recommended, otherwise q_BN is limited to the upper bound of Eq. 10-14. The resistance factor phi = 0.50 specified in AASHTO (2007) was set by fitting to FS = 2.75 with the reliability-based factors of Paikowsky et al. (2004) (Allen, 2005). Bearing capacity theory may be used instead, but because the displacement to mobilize full base resistance varies widely, Eq. 10-14 is recommended for routine design.

sections.title: Cohesive Soils
sections.body: SIDE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-15 to 10-18]. Short-term undrained side resistance in cohesive layers is in terms of undrained shear strength: R_SN = pi B Delta z f_SN = pi B Delta z (alpha s_u) (Eq. 10-15), s_u the average undrained shear strength over Delta z and alpha the adhesion coefficient (the 'alpha method'). Laboratory strength tests of undisturbed samples are recommended for s_u; in-situ tests should be calibrated against laboratory tests. UC and UU tests are less reliable than CIUC triaxial tests (sample disturbance, strain rate, drainage), so UC and UU values are first converted to CIUC (Chen and Kulhawy, 1993): s_u(UC)/s_u(CIUC) = 0.893 + 0.513 log(s_u(UC)/sigma'_vo) (Eq. 10-16); s_u(UU)/s_u(CIUC) = 0.911 + 0.499 log(s_u(UU)/sigma'_vo) (Eq. 10-17), sigma'_vo the vertical effective stress. The adhesion factor (Chen et al., 2011; Figure 10-6), recommended as a revision to the expressions in AASHTO LRFD (2017a), is alpha = 0.30 + 0.17 / (s_u(CIUC)/p_a) (Eq. 10-18), p_a atmospheric pressure in consistent units. It is common practice to neglect side resistance over the top 5 ft of the shaft, or to the depth of seasonal moisture change, subject to local experience. Permanent casing through cohesive soil reduces side resistance; reduction factors of 50 to 75 percent for steel piles compared with driven concrete piles are a guide, with no specific data for cased shafts, which may sit near the lower end. Illustrative Example 10-2 [p. 10-18]: a stiff clay layer of 27 ft with mean s_u = 2,000 psf (UU): sigma'_vo = 3,697 psf, s_u/sigma'_vo = 0.541, s_u(CIUC) = 2,000 / (0.911 + 0.499 log 0.541) = 2,571 psf (as printed), alpha = 0.30 + 0.17/(2,571/2,116) = 0.44, f_SN = 1,131 psf, R_SN,3 = 479.7 kips. The alpha method assumes design for short-term undrained loading by total stress is adequate for routine design; for very heavily overconsolidated clay (OCR > 8) the fully drained side resistance may be considered, using Eq. 10-5 with c' = 0, phi' from CD or CU triaxial tests, the interface friction angle taken equal to phi', and K = K_o from in-situ measurements or OCR. No resistance factor is recommended for fully drained side resistance in cohesive soils. BASE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-19, 10-20]. Total stress bearing capacity (O'Neill and Reese, 1999): q_BN = N*_c s_u (Eq. 10-19), s_u the mean undrained shear strength over a depth of 2B below the base. For depth at least 3 times the diameter and s_u at least 2,000 psf, N*_c = 9.0; for smaller s_u, N*_c is taken from Table 10-2 (500 psf: 6.5; 1,000 psf: 8.0; 2,000 psf and above: 9.0; linear interpolation between). For embedment D < 3B: q_BN = (2/3) [1 + D/(6B)] N*_c s_u (Eq. 10-20), N*_c from Table 10-2. The resistance factor phi = 0.40 (Table 8-4) for base resistance by this method is based on Allen (2005), fitting to ASD FS = 2.75 and the reliability analysis of Paikowsky et al. (2004). Fully drained base resistance in heavily overconsolidated clay (OCR > 8) can be analysed by bearing capacity theory with c' and phi'; it is not addressed in AASHTO (2017a). Example 10-3 [p. 10-20]: q_BN = 9.0 (2,571 psf) = 23.1 ksf, R_BN = pi/4 (5 ft)^2 x 23.1 ksf = 453.6 kips.

sections.title: Rock
sections.body: SIDE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-20 to 10-22]. Unit side resistance in rock is evaluated from the mean uniaxial compressive strength q_u of the rock layer: f_SN / p_a = C sqrt(q_u / p_a) (Eq. 10-21), p_a atmospheric pressure in the units of q_u and C a regression coefficient from load test results. Kulhawy et al. (2005), the most recent regression of load test data, give a mean C = 1.0; Eq. 10-21 with C = 1.0 is recommended for 'normal' rock sockets. q_u should come from laboratory uniaxial compression tests (ASTM) on specimens at field moisture content; estimating q_u from point load or Schmidt hammer tests may be inappropriate, and specimens allowed to dry give higher q_u and overestimate resistance. The q_u used in Eq. 10-21 should not exceed the compressive strength of the shaft concrete, unless load tests demonstrate higher side resistance. 'Normal' means sockets constructed with conventional equipment with nominally clean sidewalls and no special procedures or artificial roughening; rock prone to smearing or rapid deterioration (clay shales; Appendix B) is outside the normal range. Rock mass that cannot be excavated without caving is also outside the normal category and may show lower side resistance than Eq. 10-21 with C = 1.0. Where caving or instability of the socket is anticipated (e.g., 'plug-ahead' or 'grout-ahead' installation), O'Neill and Reese (1999) is recommended: f_SN / p_a = 0.65 alpha_E sqrt(q_u / p_a) (Eq. 10-22), with alpha_E from the RQD and the joint condition in Table 10-3. Table 10-3, side resistance reduction factor for caving rock, joint modification factor alpha_E [p. 10-21]: RQD 100 percent: 1.00 (closed joints), 0.85 (open or gouge-filled joints); RQD 70: 0.85, 0.55; RQD 50: 0.60, 0.55; RQD 30: 0.50, 0.50; RQD 20: 0.45, 0.45. In summary, Eq. 10-21 with C = 1.0 is recommended for routine design of rock sockets; for highly fractured or weathered rock that cannot be drilled without artificial support (casing or the plug-ahead method), or where caving is anticipated, Eq. 10-22 with the Table 10-3 reduction factors is recommended. The resistance factor recommended with Eqs. 10-21 and 10-22 is phi = 0.55, based on fitting to ASD with FS = 2.5, 'as presented in Table 8-4' (p. 10-21; Table 8-4 on p. 8-14 prints 0.50 for side resistance in rock: the library's table_8_4_resistance_factor returns the table's 0.50 with a note quoting p. 10-21). [pp. 10-21, 10-22] Artificial roughening of sockets (grooving tools or other measures) can increase side resistance; regression of load test data by Kulhawy and Prakoso (2007) suggests a mean value C = 1.9 with use of Eq. 10-22 for roughened sockets. It is strongly recommended that load tests or local experience be used to verify values of C greater than 1.0. BASE RESISTANCE [pp. 10-22 to 10-25]. q_BN = N*_cr q_u (Eq. 10-23), N*_cr an empirical bearing capacity factor for rock. Prakoso and Kulhawy (2002; Figure 10-7): 14 load tests at 9 sites, mean N*_cr = 3.38, COV = 35.4 percent; a lower bound N*_cr = 2.5 (consistent with Rowe and Armitage, 1987) incorporates most points; the Zhang and Einstein (1998) data give a mean 3.56, COV = 61.0 percent. N*_cr = 2.5 is recommended when q_u is the only parameter used and (1) the base bears on massive or tightly jointed rock (no compressible seams or joints) to at least one diameter below the base, (2) no solution cavities or voids exist beneath the base, and (3) a clean base can be achieved and verified. The AASHTO (2017a) resistance factor for Eq. 10-23 with N*_cr = 2.5 is phi = 0.50 (FS = 2.5); larger N*_cr is justified when verified by local experience or load testing. For fractured rock mass, bearing capacity with the Hoek-Brown criterion (Turner and Ramey, 2010): sigma'_1 = sigma'_3 + q_u [m_b (sigma'_3/q_u) + s]^a (Eq. 10-24); with GSI, m_b/m_i = exp[(GSI - 100)/28] (Eq. 10-25), s = exp[(GSI - 100)/9] (Eq. 10-26), a = 1/2 + (1/6)[exp(-GSI/15) - exp(-20/3)] (Eq. 10-27). The overburden parameter A = sigma'_vb + q_u [m_b (sigma'_vb/q_u) + s]^a (Eq. 10-28), sigma'_vb the vertical effective stress at the socket tip; q_BN = A + q_u [m_b (A/q_u) + s]^a (Eq. 10-29). N*_cr = 2.5 can be used as an upper bound on base resistance unless local experience or load tests validate higher values (Figure 10-8). The recommended resistance factor for Eq. 10-29 is phi = 0.50 (FS = 2.5). [p. 10-25] Base resistance may instead be governed by the structural strength of the concrete in bearing (Chapter 12); the structural bearing resistance factor is phi = 0.70 against the geotechnical phi = 0.50, so the factored resistances are compared case by case. Example 10-4 [pp. 10-26 to 10-28]: 6 ft socket, 10 ft deep, q_u = 2,500 psi (360 ksf): f_SN = 2.116 x 1.0 x sqrt(300/2.116) = 27.6 ksf as printed (the printed expression evaluates to 25.2 ksf; the printed R_SN follows the 27.6), R_SN = 27.6 x (6 pi) x 10 = 5,202 kips; q_BN = 2.5 (360) = 900 ksf, R_BN = 25,447 kips, phi R_BN = 0.50 (25,447) = 12,723 kips, governing over the structural 19,380 kips.

sections.body: [pp. 10-28, 10-29] Step 6 applies resistance factors to the nominal resistances of Step 5 and checks each strength limit state from Step 2, for each loading mode and each trial design, against Eq. 10-1: Sum(eta_i gamma_i F_i) <= Sum(phi_i R_i). Recommended resistance factors for the nominal resistances calculated by the methods above are in Table 8-4. When compressive resistances are determined from one or more static load tests, AASHTO (2017a) allows a resistance factor as high as 0.70; the value selected is a matter of engineering judgment and accounts for the number of load tests and the subsurface variability (Chapter 13). Illustrative Example 10-5 [p. 10-29]: factored demand Sum(gamma Q) = 766 kips (Strength I). Factors from Table 8-4 as used in the example: side resistance in compression, cohesionless soil 0.55; cohesive soil 0.45; base resistance, cohesive soil 0.40. Factored resistances: layer 1 197.2 x 0.55 = 108.5 kips; layer 2 635.6 x 0.55 = 349.6 kips; layer 3 side 479.7 x 0.45 = 215.9 kips; layer 3 base 453.6 x 0.40 = 181.4 kips; Sum(phi R) = 855.4 kips. 766 kips < 855.4 kips; C/D = 855.4/766 = 1.12 > 1.0, so the trial design satisfies the strength limit state.

sections.title: Evaluate Trial Design for Service Limit States (Step 7)
sections.body: [pp. 10-30 to 10-37] Settlement criteria reflect structure function and type, service life and consequences of movement. Studies of tolerable bridge settlement (Moulton et al., 1985; Barker et al., 1991) led to rules of thumb such as an angular distortion between adjacent foundations of 0.008 radians in simple spans and 0.004 in continuous spans, but movement criteria are set per project with the structural engineer; a survey reported by Paikowsky et al. (2004) found tolerable bridge foundation settlement typically 0.25 to 2.0 inches. In LRFD terms the service limit state is the axial resistance at the tolerable deformation delta_service, checked by Sum(eta_i gamma_i F_i) <= Sum(phi_i R_i) (Eq. 10-30) with R_i the resistances at that deformation and phi_i and gamma_i currently taken as 1.0 (AASHTO, 2017a). Three methods are given: a simple hand method from field load tests (preliminary design, or showing settlement is not critical); numerical simulation of load transfer (layered soil and rock, planning load tests, cases where settlement may govern); and closed-form solutions for shafts on or socketed into rock or very dense geomaterials (details in Appendix C). COHESIONLESS AND COHESIVE SOILS, SIMPLE METHOD [pp. 10-30 to 10-35]: load test data normalized by the nominal resistance and plotted against displacement normalized by B give an average curve, a crude first-order estimate given the scatter, suited to preliminary analyses or checking whether deformation matters. The earlier O'Neill and Reese (1999) separate side and base curves are in Appendix C; Figure 10-10, adapted from Chen and Kulhawy (2002) from a worldwide database of compression tests on straight-sided shafts (46 data points for cohesionless and 56 for cohesive soils), combines both. Each curve is linear to delta/B = 0.4% at 50% normalized force, nonlinear between 0.4% and 4.0%, where the force at 4.0% is the interpreted failure threshold, and beyond it constant at 100% for cohesive soils and still rising for cohesionless soils. The axial force includes the shaft weight W; for cohesive soils the failure threshold is R_SN + R_BN, and for cohesionless soils R_SN plus the base resistance at delta/B = 4.0%, so the Eq. 10-14 base resistance (developed at 5 percent) is multiplied by 0.71. The data cover diameters 1 ft to 6.5 ft, depths 16 ft to 200 ft and depth/diameter 5.8 to 56.4, and use of the curves is limited to those ranges; displacements are butt displacements, including elastic shortening. Procedure: (1) failure threshold = R_SN + R_BN = Q_c + W (Eq. 10-31; the step cites 'Step 11-6' and the text 'Equation 10-30', as printed), W being the effective weight (total above and buoyant below the water table); (2) R_SN and R_BN from 10.3.5.2 for cohesive soils, and for cohesionless soils beta-method side resistance (10.3.5.1) and 0.71 times the Eq. 10-14 base resistance; (3) normalize the tolerable settlement, delta_service/B in percent; (4) read the normalized force from Figure 10-10; (5) multiply by the failure threshold to get the axial compressive force = R_service + W and subtract W; (6) use R_service in the right side of Eq. 10-1. Chen and Kulhawy (2002) used the beta method, the alpha method and bearing capacity theory for cohesive base resistance ('the methods presented in Section 13.3.3', as printed). The curves are average behavior, not rigorous predictions; in mixed profiles the base soil type sets the base resistance and the curve to use. Illustrative Example 10-6 [pp. 10-33 to 10-35]: the trial shaft of Examples 10-1 to 10-5, Service I tolerable settlement 1.5 inch under 575 kips; R_SN = 197.2 + 635.6 + 479.7 = 1,312.5 kips, R_BN = 453.6 kips, W = pi/4 (5 ft)^2 [15 ft (150 pcf) + 45 ft (150 - 62.4 pcf)] = 121,580 lb = 121.6 kips; failure threshold 1,766.1 kips; delta/B = 1.5/60 = 2.5%, normalized load 93% on the cohesive curve (Figure 10-11; 'Figure 13-10' in the step, as printed); R_service + W = 0.93 (1,766.1) = 1,642.5 kips, R_service = 1,521 kips > 575 kips, easily satisfied. Expected settlement: (575 + 121.6)/1,766 = 0.39 = 39 percent, normalized displacement 0.40% x (39/50) = 0.31%, settlement 0.0031 x 60 = 0.19 inch, under 0.2 inch. NUMERICAL SIMULATION OF LOAD TRANSFER [pp. 10-35 to 10-36]: for layered profiles or many load cases, the shaft is a linear spring and each layer a nonlinear t-z spring (cantilever spring and friction block), with a q-w_b spring at the base (Figure 10-12); the governing differential equation (Appendix D) is solved numerically, usually by finite differences, in commercial software. Accuracy depends entirely on the t-z and q-w_b curves, which research cannot yet predict with confidence for all conditions and which may depend on construction; on major projects instrumented design-phase load tests calibrate site-specific curves, assuming production shafts are built with similar methods and tools. APPROXIMATE CLOSED-FORM SOLUTIONS [pp. 10-36 to 10-37]: spreadsheet solutions for shafts in rock or very dense geomaterials, agreeing with elastic-plastic theory, finite element analysis and load test back-analysis, predict the top-of-socket displacement w_c under Q_c for an elastic cylinder (depth D, diameter B, E_c, nu_c) in rock mass (E_r, nu_r) over base rock (E_b, nu_b), with average axial stress sigma_b = 4Q_c/(pi B^2) (Figure 10-13); cases: rock-socketed shafts (Carter and Kulhawy, 1988) and shafts in dense cohesionless soils with SPT N-values > 50 (Mayne and Harris, 1993). The equations and inputs are given in Appendix C, the solutions in Appendix D (both as printed).

sections.title: Design for Uplift
sections.body: [pp. 10-37 to 10-40] Uplift arises, for example, where moment on a pier footing is resisted by a couple of uplift in shafts on one side and compression in shafts on the other (Figure 10-14), and from construction loads, adjacent-span loading, seismic and impact events. A shaft in uplift is resisted by its weight and by side resistance on the shaft-geomaterial interface (Figure 10-15). AASHTO (2017a) requires uplift resistance of a single straight-sided shaft to be estimated in a manner similar to side resistance in compression, so nominal unit side resistances come from the methods of Section 10.3.5. Base resistance (tip suction) is not relied on: its prediction is not sufficiently reliable. The shaft weight is treated as a negative force effect on the left side of Eq. 10-1, not as resistance, so the strength limit state is Sum(phi_i R_i) = Sum over i = 1 to n of phi_S,i R_SN,i (numbered 10-32 in the print, p. 10-39). Resistance factors for uplift side resistance are in Table 8-4; the uplift values are less by 0.10 than the equivalent compression factors (Allen, 2005; AASHTO, 2017a), an interim procedure pending reliability-based calibration. Where side resistance comes from one or more static uplift load tests at the site, AASHTO (2017a) allows phi = 0.60 for all geomaterials, applied with judgment on how well production shafts match the test conditions; otherwise a lower factor is used. If the uplift is caused by an extreme event (earthquake, ice, vessel impact), the uplift resistance factor can be taken as 0.80 (p. 10-40).

sections.title: Background and Definitions
sections.body: [p. 10-40] Bridge scour is the loss of soil by erosion from water flowing around bridge supports. Total scour at a highway crossing comprises (1) long-term aggradation and degradation of the river bed, (2) contraction scour at the bridge and (3) local scour at piers or abutments. Aggradation is the progressive buildup of the channel bed by sediment deposition and degradation its progressive lowering by erosion, both predicted to occur without the bridge. Contraction is narrowing of the channel by bridge construction or other factors, and contraction scour the removal of material across all or most of the channel width from the increased velocity. Local scour is erosion around obstacles from localized flow acceleration and vortices, at piers and abutments. Total scour is the sum of long-term degradation, contraction scour and local scour (Figure 10-16). Effects for drilled shaft design: changes in subsurface stress, reduced embedment and geotechnical resistances, and possible changes in structure response and foundation force effects. Channel migration, the lateral migration of an alluvial channel across its floodplain by bank erosion and point bar deposition, is not a specific scour component but can likewise remove or build up soil at piers and abutments.

sections.title: Design Philosophy for Scour
sections.body: [pp. 10-40 to 10-42] HEC-18, 'Evaluating Scour at Bridges' (Arneson et al., 2012), gives practical scour analysis methods and design procedures. Foundations for new bridges should withstand scour from floods larger than the hydraulic design flood, which the Owner selects on a risk basis; the minimum scour design flood and scour design check flood then follow Table 10-4 (QD = flood with a return interval of D years): hydraulic design Q10, scour design Q25, check Q50; Q25, Q50, Q100; Q50, Q100, Q200; Q100, Q200, Q500. Both scour floods exceed the hydraulic design flood, because that flood has a reasonably high likelihood of being exceeded in the service life and greater scour could cause failure, and for redundancy. Bridges must not fail under the worst conditions of the scour design flood and should be checked not to fail under the scour design check flood; the check flood is an extreme event, the scour design flood is not, and its scour applies to all strength and service limit states. Concepts: (1) design by an interdisciplinary team with hydraulic, geotechnical and structural expertise; (2) hydraulic studies are a necessary part of bridge design, covering waterway opening size (for upstream and downstream landowners and safe foundations) and scour calculations, scoped to the complexity, highway importance and consequences of failure; (3) scour formulas have limitations, so results are compared by judgment with site data: performance of existing structures in past floods, regulation and control of flood discharges, hydrologic characteristics and flood history, structural redundancy, and historical channel migration; (4) approach damage from rare floods is quickly repaired, but scour collapse or major damage creates safety hazards and long social and economic losses, so a higher hydraulic standard is warranted for foundations than for approaches.

sections.title: Analysis and Prediction of Scour
sections.body: [pp. 10-42 to 10-43] Scour is addressed in three stages: (1) a stream stability and geomorphic assessment per HEC-20, 'Stream Stability at Highway Structures' (Lagasse et al., 2012); (2) a scour analysis per HEC-18 (Arneson et al., 2012), which includes foundation design and is most relevant to drilled shafts (flow chart, Figure 10-17), existing scour-critical bridges going to a new design or Stage 3; (3) a plan of action for countermeasures, not applicable to new designs. Hydrologic and hydraulic analyses are usually by a hydraulic specialist with geotechnical input (subsurface profiles from borings and geophysics, USCS classification, erodibility of units), structural input (number, location and geometry of piers and abutments) and civil input (approach embankment limits, hydraulic structures through them). A scour prism is developed for each pier and abutment, and the team evaluates strength, service and extreme event limit states of the foundations with the scour prism removed; if unstable, the design is modified (longer bridge, longer spans, number, size and arrangement of shafts) or countered. Foundations are generally designed for the predicted scour rather than relying on measures such as rip-rap, whose long-term effectiveness is typically unreliable. Methods for degradation, contraction and local scour are in HEC-18 and not repeated; the principal output is the scour prism, the total volume removed by scour.

sections.title: Application to Drilled Shaft Design
sections.body: [pp. 10-43 to 10-44] AASHTO (2017a) requires two scour conditions: design flood scour for strength and service limit states, and check flood scour for the extreme limit state. The commentary to Article 10.5.5.2.1: 'Scour design for the design flood must satisfy the requirement that the factored foundation resistance after scour is greater than the factored load determined with the scoured soil removed. The resistance factors will be those used in the Strength Limit State, without scour.' So the Table 8-4 resistance factors apply to strength limit states under design flood scour, and the Table 8-4 Extreme Event II factors to the check flood. For each strength or service evaluation all material in the scour prism above the total scour line is removed and unavailable for axial or lateral support; the stress changes differ for scour over a large area (degradation and contraction) and a small area (local scour), the degraded and contracted streambed having the greater influence on stresses along the embedded length where local scour is limited. In Figure 10-18 the streambed drops from point A to point B by degradation plus contraction scour, with a local scour hole of depth ys (HEC-18) and a suggested top width w of 2.0 ys on each side of the pier (Arneson et al., 2012). Vertical stress is zero at the top of the embedded length (point C), is controlled by streambed elevation B at embedment of 1.5 ys or more, and varies linearly over the depth 1.5 ys.

sections.title: Effects of Scour on Axial Resistance
sections.body: [p. 10-45] Scour enters the beta-method side resistance in cohesionless soils (10.3.5.1) through sigma'_v in f_SN = sigma'_v beta (Eq. 10-7, reprinted), so the vertical stress changes of Figure 10-18 are applied over the portion in cohesionless layers. In cohesive soils (alpha method, 10.3.5.2) su and unit side resistance can be assumed unchanged by scour, and rock strength and resistances likewise. Other issues: column action from the longer unsupported length after scour; overlapping local scour holes at piers and abutments make scour indeterminate and possibly deeper, the top width on each side ranging from 1.0 to 2.8 times the local scour depth, 2.0 suggested; placing the top of a shaft-supported footing or cap below the streambed at the long-term degradation plus contraction scour depth minimizes obstruction and local scour, lower still where shafts could be eroded by river or tidal currents, though in deep water a cap at or above the mudline or at the waterline may be more cost effective; stub abutments in the embankment should be on shafts or piles extending below the thalweg (lowest streambed elevation) including long-term degradation and contraction scour, in case the thalweg shifts; and contraction and local scour estimates must consider any foundation cap and pier protection system.

sections.title: Downdrag
sections.body: [p. 10-45] Downdrag: 10.6.1 Occurrence; 10.6.2 Downdrag - Basic Concepts and Analysis; 10.6.3 Strategies to Address Downdrag.
key_points: Subsections: occurrence, neutral plane concepts and analysis, strategies
sections.applicability: Drilled shafts in settling soils; fills over soft ground; post-liquefaction conditions

sections.title: Occurrence
sections.body: [pp. 10-45 to 10-47] Downdrag is the downward movement of a deep foundation from drag loads transferred by shear from surrounding soil that moves down (settlement or slope movement); Briaud and Tucker (1997) note reports of 'extreme movements, differential settlements, and extensive damage' including highway bridges. Bridge abutments (Figure 10-19) are a common case: shafts, abutment and then fill, with settlement of fill (virtually any fill compresses with time, especially if poorly compacted) and of native soil under the fill, time-dependent in clay, which may also squeeze laterally against the shafts. Settling soils include loose sand (also from cyclic loading by earthquakes, traffic or groundwater fluctuation), soft to medium stiff clay, recent fill and liquefied soils; fill such as an approach embankment or lowered groundwater can induce consolidation long after installation. Briaud and Tucker (1997) criteria, any one requiring downdrag consideration: total ground settlement over 4 inches; settlement after installation over 0.4 inch; embankment height over 6 ft; compressible layer thicker than 30 ft. AASHTO (2017a) includes drag load DD in Strength I through V (Tables 8-2 and 8-3), implying it is resisted at both geotechnical and structural strength limits; this manual differs, concluding that drag forces are non-existent at the geotechnical strength limit, since the shaft movement to reach it would exceed the soil's, and should be limited to the structural strength limit state. For a shaft bearing in hard or stiff material drag can fully develop and factored drag loads are included for the structural check, though they are unlikely to control a solid reinforced concrete shaft. The tip elevation is typically controlled by penetrating through the strata causing downdrag. DD is also in the AASHTO Service I combinations, and downward movement is addressed in the geotechnical service limit state.

sections.title: Downdrag - Basic Concepts and Analysis
sections.body: [pp. 10-47 to 10-48] The neutral plane is the depth above which the shaft carries drag forces and below which it develops resistance to the downward forces, the structure load plus drag load (Fellenius, 2006); establishing it is essential in any downdrag analysis. In Figure 10-20 Curve A is the nominal resistance Rn minus side resistance with depth and Curve B the sustained top load Q plus downdrag (assumed equal to side resistance); the neutral plane is at their intersection. The FHWA approach is in Section 7.3.6.1 of GEC 12 (Hannigan et al., 2016), the neutral plane method of Fellenius (1989) modified by Siegel et al. (2013), in LRFD form for the structural strength and geotechnical service limit states, needing the nominal sustained load at the shaft top, stratigraphy and layer parameters, load-deformation models (instrumented load tests, or t-z and q-z models) and fill placement amount, extent and timeline. Nominal unit drag load f_DN uses the 10.3.5 side resistance methods: beta for cohesionless soils, alpha for short-term undrained cohesive soils, and effective stress for long-term cohesive conditions where appropriate. Post-liquefaction drag is in 10.7 and groups in Chapter 11.

sections.title: Strategies to Address Downdrag
sections.body: [p. 10-49] Axial resistance can be increased by increasing shaft size or adding shafts; a larger diameter attracts more drag load, while added length adds resistance without more drag and is more effective in most cases. Measures to reduce downdrag (Briaud and Tucker, 1997, for driven piles, also applicable): preloading to induce settlement before construction; lightweight fill to reduce surface load; permanent steel casing, with or without coating, to reduce adhesion in the downdrag zone; preventing contact with the compressible soils, e.g., permanent double casing with the annulus filled with a material such as styrofoam beads, limited to cases where lateral loading is not significant; and ground improvement to stiffen compressible layers. A larger diameter with fewer shafts in a group could reduce total downdrag on the foundation. Both approaches (changing the shafts or reducing settlement) should be considered and chosen on cost, constructability and project requirements.
key_points: Lengthening adds resistance without more drag; widening attracts more drag
Reduce downdrag: preloading, lightweight fill, permanent casing, double casing with styrofoam annulus, ground improvement
Compare shaft changes with settlement reduction on cost and constructability

sections.title: Seismic Considerations
sections.body: [pp. 10-49 to 10-52] LRFD seismic analysis and design of bridges is in the NHI manual by Marsh et al. (2014). The AASHTO Extreme Event I combination includes EQ; the structural engineer provides the factored axial demands and the shafts are designed to Eq. 10-1, using the 10.3.5 resistances with four seismic issues: effective stress reduction from excess pore pressure, liquefaction or cyclic softening, post-liquefaction downdrag, and extreme event resistance factors. EFFECTIVE STRESS [pp. 10-50 to 10-51]: in saturated loose granular soils excess pore pressure reduces sigma'_v and so beta-method side resistance (Eq. 10-7) even without liquefaction, to be considered for cohesionless layers at Extreme Event I. With r_u = Delta u / sigma'_v0 (Eq. 10-33), liquefaction occurs as r_u approaches 1; for 0 <= r_u < 1 the modified beta method f_SN = sigma'_v0 (1 - r_u) beta = sigma'_v0 (1 - r_u) K_o tan(delta) (Eq. 10-34; Boulanger and Brandenberg, 2004) applies, other parameters as pre-earthquake. r_u for FS_liq > 1 (triggering per Chapter 9) can be estimated from the Marcuson et al. (1990) fit r_u = 1/[1 + 15(FS_liq - 1.0)] (Eq. 10-35) or, since shear strain relates more closely to pore pressure generation, from gamma_max by Cetin and Bilge (2012) (Eq. 10-36, D_R in percent), shown by them to predict r_u more accurately than stress-based approaches. Apply to layers with FS_liq between 1.0 and 1.5; above 1.5 significant pore pressure is not expected, though the limit could be raised for critical projects in high seismic regions; for r_u close to 1.0 take a lower bound side resistance equal to the residual undrained strength su,r (Chapter 9). STRENGTH REDUCTIONS [pp. 10-51 to 10-52]: liquefied soil resistance (some fraction of su,r) can be taken as zero at Extreme Event I; blast tests by Rollins et al. (2018) confirmed essentially zero side resistance in liquefied soil and about pre-shaking side resistance in non-liquefied layers above, but AASHTO (2017a) 10.8.4 neglects side resistance in all layers above a liquefied zone; this likely underestimates resistance, but the tests are too limited for a general rule, so engineers should use judgment before neglecting it, particularly for thick non-liquefied soil over a thin liquefied layer. A shaft tip should never bear immediately above or in a liquefiable layer, which may govern tip elevation. Cyclic softening of saturated cohesive soils (Chu et al., 2008), most in sensitive low-OCR clays, can be approximated with the alpha method using 80 percent of the CIUC su (10.3.5.2); explicit procedures (Idriss and Boulanger, 2008) are rarely warranted except for major structures in critical seismic zones. POST-LIQUEFACTION DOWNDRAG [p. 10-52]: reconsolidation of liquefied layers and settlement of overlying layers cause drag loads, maximum at the end of reconsolidation (settlement after Ishihara and Yoshimine, 1992, in Idriss and Boulanger, 2008); drag from previously liquefied layers is 50 percent of the pre-earthquake beta-method side resistance (Rollins et al., 2018), and static side resistance above the liquefied zone. AASHTO (2017a) includes these DD loads as permanent loads in Extreme Event I with a load factor of 1.0 (consolidation drag excluded), but since reconsolidation occurs hours or days after shaking this appears misguided, and post-liquefaction drag loads should be considered only for structural strength and service limit states (10.6). EXTREME EVENT I RESISTANCE FACTORS [p. 10-52]: in Eq. 10-1, 1.0 for compression and 0.80 for uplift of single shafts under earthquake loading, the lower uplift value reflecting greater uncertainty in side-only resistance.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: [p. 10-52] Axial design is one of the major steps of the overall design and construction process (Chapter 8). The chapter presents concepts and methods for LRFD design of single drilled shafts under axial loading, equations for nominal side and base resistance for each geomaterial category, examples of LRFD limit state checks in axial compression, and an idealized load-settlement model based on load test observations for evaluating the Service I limit state of shafts in soil; more rigorous load-displacement methods are in Appendix C.
